newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak bank mulls subordinated debt issue.
newsitem.headline: Slovak bank mulls subordinated debt issue.

text.p: Slovenska Sporitelna a.s., looking to break new ground in central Europe, said on Wednesday it is mulling an international subordinated debt issue to help raise its basic capital by one half.

Ivan Benda, Sporitelna's Treasury Director, told Reuters that if successful, the issue could "certainly be the first" such deal among banks in central Europe and would help raise the bank's profile abroad.
"Subordinated debt is the only way we can get the (capital adequacy) ratio we should have," Benda said. "It (issue) may not be this year, but it may be next year."
"Undercapitalisation is one of the weak points of our bank, but it will be soon resolved," he added.
Benda said that though negotiations with international banks were "permanently ongoing", the issue had yet to be approved and to detail its strategy was "premature".
Sporitelna's capital adequacy stands at 7.25 percent, after 6.94 percent in 1994, and the aim is to riase it to 8.0 percent next year, Benda said.
To achieve that, the bank's current basic capital of five billion crowns should be increased by two to three billion slovak crowns ($65.2-$97.8 million), Benda added.

"In the present situation, our capital appears to be low for the capital adeqacy calculation considering the past and an expansion of future commercial activities of the bank. We need to strengthen it," Benda said.
The activities included loans, bills of exchange, international payments and such, and were directed inside and outside of the country, he said.

The other possible way for Sporitelna to increase its capital was via a share issue, Benda said but "our capital increase is a problem, because the National Property Fund (NPF) has so far not considered such a possibility".
The NPF, a state privatisation agency, is currently the sole owner of Sporitelna.
Parliament has postponed privatisation of the country's financial institutions through to the end of next March, and once resumed, it would involve domestic investors only.
However, Benda said the subordinated debt issue "should be interesting" to parties other than the bank's current owner.
He added that last year the subordinated debt issue alternative was negotiated with domestic institutions and "no good agreement was reached".
